method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: **FSS are real physical symptoms** from altered brain–body or nervous-system functioning, not structural disease. **They are not imagined, exaggerated, deliberate or under conscious control.**
claims.source_text: Functional somatic symptoms (FSS) are common, real physical symptoms arising from altered brain-body or nervous system functioning rather than structural disease. Symptoms are not imagined, exaggerated, deliberate or under conscious control
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **FSS can co-exist with medical conditions** and may be triggered or worsened by illness, injury, stress or developmental factors.
claims.source_text: FSS can co-exist with medical conditions and may be triggered or exacerbated by illness, injury, stress or developmental factors
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Not malingering or factitious disorder.** Psychological and social factors may contribute but **are not required for the diagnosis.**
claims.source_text: FSS are not the result of malingering, factitious disorder, or conscious fabrication psychological and social factors may contribute to symptom onset or persistence, but are not required for diagnosis
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Unnecessary investigations and fragmented care can worsen symptoms** and functional impairment.
claims.source_text: Unnecessary investigations and fragmented care can inadvertently worsen symptoms and functional impairment
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Neurodivergent children may need early specialist input**, as communication differences, sensory sensitivities and overlapping symptoms can change presentation and management.
claims.source_text: Children with neurodivergence may require early specialist input as communication differences, sensory sensitivities, and overlapping functional symptoms may influence presentation and management
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Approach:** screen for red flags → identify positive features → minimal investigations → explain the diagnosis → functional rehabilitation plan.
claims.source_text: Assess and screen for red flags Identify positive features Minimal investigations Explain diagnosis Functional rehabilitation plan
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **History:** symptom pattern and triggers; psychosocial assessment (children and families) or **HEADSSS** (adolescents); functional impact on school, social life, activity and mobility; medications; past and family history of FSS; development.
claims.source_text: Symptom characteristics, ie location, time course, triggers, fluctuation, what improves and worsens symptoms Current psychosocial assessment (children and their families) or HEADSSS screen (adolescents) Functional impact of symptoms, eg school attendance, work, social activities and relationships, physical activity, activities of daily living, mobility
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Examine thoroughly** to confirm FSS and to exclude reversible or serious organic contributors.
claims.source_text: General screening examination to confirm diagnosis of FSS and to exclude any reversible and/or serious organic contributors to the symptoms
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Red flags:** persistent consistent focal deficits · progressive symptoms without fluctuation · weight loss, growth failure or persistent fever · symptoms waking the child at night · **syncope with exertion or cardiac symptoms** · reproducible, congruent abnormal neurology · new seizures concerning for epilepsy.
claims.source_text: The following features warrant careful assessment and may require further investigation or referral persistent, consistent focal neurological deficits progressive symptoms without fluctuation objective weight loss, growth failure, or persistent fever nocturnal symptoms that wake child from sleep syncope associated with exertion or cardiac symptoms abnormal neurological examination that is reproducible and congruent new onset seizures with features concerning for epilepsy
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Red flags do not exclude FSS** but may indicate co-existing pathology.
claims.source_text: The presence of red flags does not exclude FSS but may indicate co-existing pathology
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Positive features:** fluctuation with context, attention or stress · inconsistency with recognised disease patterns · variable examination · **improvement with distraction** · impairment out of proportion to findings · co-existing fatigue, pain, sleep or autonomic symptoms · hyperventilation · repeated low-yield presentations.
claims.source_text: Symptoms that fluctuate over time, context, attention, or stress Inconsistency between symptoms and recognised disease patterns Variability in examination findings Symptoms that improve with distraction or automatic movement Marked functional impairment disproportionate to objective findings Co-existing fatigue, pain, sleep disturbance, or autonomic symptoms Hyperventilation on clinical assessment Recurrent healthcare presentations with limited diagnostic yield
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Make the diagnosis positive, proportionate and collaborative**; it does not require exhaustive exclusion of all organic disease.
claims.source_text: Diagnosis of FSS should be Positive, based on identifiable clinical features Proportionate, ensuring safety while avoiding excessive testing Collaborative, with clear explanation provided to the child and family Diagnosis does not require exhaustive exclusion of all possible organic disease
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Refer early for multidisciplinary (including mental health) assessment** if symptoms need admission, cause significant sustained impairment such as school non-attendance, the team disagrees on the diagnosis, there is social complexity or risk (e.g. family violence), or there is concern that symptoms are intentionally produced.
claims.source_text: Consider early referral for multidisciplinary assessment (including mental health assessment) if symptoms are causing enough distress and/or functional impairment to require admission significant or sustained functional impairment due to symptoms (eg non-attendance at school, loss of social connections) a lack of consensus within the treating team regarding a diagnosis of FSS social complexity and/or complex risk (eg exposure to family violence, bereavement, food or housing insecurity) concern that symptoms are being intentionally produced
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **No test confirms FSS. Investigations are generally not required**, and should stop once a functional diagnosis is made unless new symptoms or red flags emerge.
claims.source_text: There are no investigations that will confirm a positive diagnosis of FSS Investigations are generally not required. They should be avoided once a functional diagnosis is established unless new symptoms/red flags emerge
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If done, make them targeted and justified.** Investigations can reinforce illness beliefs, raise anxiety, delay recovery and cause iatrogenic harm.
claims.source_text: targeted and clinically justified focused on excluding serious or reversible conditions … Investigations can reinforce illness beliefs increase anxiety delay recovery lead to iatrogenic harm
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Document and share results with every clinician involved**; agreeing which results would prompt reassessment helps.
claims.source_text: Investigation results should be clearly documented and shared with all clinicians involved. Identifying results that would prompt reassessment can be helpful
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A clear, confident explanation is a core treatment:** name the diagnosis as FSS, explain it as nervous-system functioning rather than damage, reassure that symptoms are real and potentially reversible, and set out a recovery plan.
claims.source_text: Clear confident explanation is a core therapeutic intervention. Key elements include naming the diagnosis clearly as FSS explaining that symptoms arise from how the nervous system is functioning, not damage reassuring that symptoms are real and potentially reversible outlining a clear plan focused on recovery and function
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Raise a suspected functional cause early**, as part of the working diagnosis; delaying it while awaiting exclusion of organic causes can be counterproductive.
claims.source_text: If a functional cause is suspected early on, it can be helpful to include this as part of the working diagnosis in discussion with the child and family at that point. Delayed introduction while awaiting the exclusion of organic causes can be counterproductive
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Many children need no multidisciplinary assessment**: acknowledge the symptoms, give a mind–body explanation that makes sense to the family, and focus on returning to usual activities despite symptoms, reassuring that this will not be harmful.
claims.source_text: Many children presenting to primary and secondary care settings with FSS do not require a multidisciplinary assessment and will respond to a management approach that includes: … A focus on functional recovery. This usually requires children to return to usual activities despite ongoing symptoms. It can be helpful to acknowledge that this may be uncomfortable and to provide some reassurance that a return to function will not be harmful and will support recovery
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **If a carer is thought to be intentionally producing the symptoms**, refer urgently to a forensic service and consider mandatory reporting.
claims.source_text: If there is concern after assessment that the symptoms are being intentionally produced by a carer, urgent referral should be made to a forensic service and consideration given to mandatory reporting responsibilities
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Treatment focuses on improving function. Early return to school is a priority**, with graded, paced activity that avoids 'boom-bust' cycles.
claims.source_text: Treatment depends on individual predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protective factors, but is primarily focused on improving function Early return to school is a priority Graded and paced activity, avoiding "boom-bust" cycles
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Symptom improvement often follows functional improvement**, not the other way round. Continuity of care avoids significant iatrogenic harm.
claims.source_text: Symptoms improvement often follows functional improvement rather than proceeding it Continuity of care can avoid significant iatrogenic harm
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Refer early to allied health** (physiotherapy for power or gait, OT for function, social work for supports) and, if the family agrees, to mental health services (e.g. CBT, family therapy). **Liaise with the school**, with letters or an individual learning plan if needed.
claims.source_text: Consider early referral to Allied Health professionals if not already engaged (eg physiotherapy for symptoms relating to muscle power or gait, occupational therapy for function and confidence, social work for linkage with community supports) Consider referral to local or community mental health services for psychological or counselling support (eg cognitive behavioural therapy, family therapy) if the child and carers are agreeable Liaise with the child's school to support attendance (may need individual learning plan in some instances) and to assess and manage any school-related contributors to the FSS. Letters can be useful
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Medicines for symptom relief, such as analgesia, are usually not effective** and should be minimised.
claims.source_text: Pharmacological treatments for symptom relief (eg analgesia) are usually not effective and should be minimised where possible
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Avoid:** repeated re-investigation · conflicting explanations · telling families 'nothing is wrong' · blaming symptoms solely on anxiety or stress · delaying diagnosis until all tests are complete.
claims.source_text: Ideally avoid repeated re-investigation once diagnosis is established conflicting explanations from different clinicians telling families "nothing is wrong" attributing symptoms solely to anxiety or stress delaying diagnosis until all tests are complete
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consult the local paediatric team** for recurrent or persistent symptoms, or red flags suggesting undiagnosed pathology.
claims.source_text: Consider consultation with local paediatric team when symptoms are recurrent or persistent history or examination indicate there may be undiagnosed pathology
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Consult CAMHS** for complex or severe symptoms, co-existing mental health problems needing acute management beyond the clinician's comfort, or **significant risk to the child or others.**
claims.source_text: Consider consultation with specialist Child and Adolescent Mental Health service when symptoms are complex, or severe there are coexisting mental health problems that require acute management and that are beyond the comfort of the clinician significant risk is identified for the child or others
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Discharge once follow-up is arranged** — GP, or community rehabilitation support such as a physiotherapist or psychologist. Plan a smooth transition to adult services for older adolescents.
claims.source_text: Consider discharge when appropriate alternative follow-up is arranged. This may include a plan for community follow-up (eg GP) or community support for functional rehabilitation (eg physiotherapist, psychologist) … Providing thoughtful and smooth transition to adult services for older adolescents is key to ongoing management and continuity of care
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Functional somatic symptoms' (Last updated June 2026), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Functional_somatic_symptoms/, retrieved 2026-09-23
